fixtures.summary: A header and nothing after it. Twelve bytes, zero sets, and it parses.
One set, four slots, one of them without a sound. A sleep timeout that reads as nonsense if it is taken big-endian.
Five sets, which is MAX_SETS. 932 bytes, the largest file that parses.
A name of exactly 32 bytes, so the field has no zero in it at all.
A name whose UTF-8 crosses the 32-byte cut, so the field ends with a lead byte and no continuation.
A sleep timeout of 0xffffffff, the largest a uint32 holds. It parses, and it is not a length of time the device can wait.
A sleep timeout of 86400 - one day, the longest the device honours as written.
A sleep timeout of 5 seconds. Below the range, and brought up to it rather than obeyed.
The reserved byte after each has-audio flag written as 0xff. A reader ignores it and reads the same fields.
The has-audio flag written as 42. Any non-zero value means the slot has a sound.
A valid one-set layout with four bytes stuck on the end. A reader ignores them.
Eleven bytes: one short of the header itself.
MTRE where MTRD belongs - one bit out in the last letter.
Version 1, the layout from before the set colour went. Refused rather than read two bytes out of step.
Version 3, from a builder newer than the device. Refused, because the reader cannot skip what it does not know.
A header claiming three slots per set on a device that has four keys.
A header claiming six sets on a device with room for five.
A header claiming two sets on a file holding one and a half.
Byte 7 set to 1, which is German. The same firmware image, a different set of words on the menu.
Byte 7 set to 7, an index no table stands behind. The layout still parses; the words fall back to English.
Every pixel spells out its own coordinates: the value at (x, y) is (y << 8) | x, so the bytes are [y, x].
32768 bytes of 0xf800: pure red, and the value that says which way round the two bytes go.
259 bytes missing, so the cut lands inside a pixel. The reader zero-fills and says nothing.
Sixteen bytes too many. The reader takes 32768 of them and never looks at the rest.
What the build writes: 16 kHz mono 16-bit PCM, fmt then data, nothing else.
A LIST chunk of odd length between fmt and data. The pad byte after it is what a reader has to step over.
A data chunk claiming four times the samples the file actually holds.
44.1 kHz stereo. The device accepts it - it never reads fmt - and plays it out at 16 kHz mono.
A file that is not a RIFF at all, under a .wav name.
A RIFF whose form is AVI rather than WAVE.
A well-formed WAV with a fmt chunk and no data chunk.
Eight bytes. Not even the RIFF header is whole.
Which names a builder may emit, which names the device will store, and the fact that the first set is inside the second.
Which language rides in which byte, what an unknown index means, and how many tables the device has to have.
The range of sleep timeouts a builder may write, what the device waits for everything else, and the fact that the first is inside the second.
Hello, list, done. The whole of what a browser learns before it decides anything.
One file across: the size and the checksum on the command line, the bytes between go and ok.
The device says two things the browser has never heard of. The browser steps over both and takes the ok.
A device one version behind this browser. It answers, and it cannot be driven.
A device one version ahead of this browser. It answers, and it cannot be driven.
A file that takes three windows, the last of them short. The browser sends what it was told and waits to be told again.
A checksum whose top byte is zero, asked for by name. Eight digits always, lower case always.
A verb from a newer browser. Answered with an error, not ignored.
Nothing gets in before a hello has been answered - and the refusal is the way back in, not the end of the session.
A name the device will not touch, a file that arrived wrong, and a file with no room for it.
One board and a key in each of the four shapes: a word with a picture, a word alone, a picture alone, and a key holding nothing.

Two boards and the ring between them, a crossed-out key sharing one picture with a plain one, a METACOM reference, a name past the 32 bytes layout.bin cuts at, and a reference behind which there is nothing.
A set with five keys in it. Four reach the package, and the fifth key's picture and recording are not in the archive at all.
A locale of "de-DE", which is not a language the device has. The reader takes it as it stands and byte 7 falls back to English.
The sleep timeout and the voice on a board that is not the root, saying something different from the root's. Only the root's are read, and the other two are lost without a word.
A key whose label is a caption and whose vocalization is the sentence. What the device says is the vocalization.
A manifest that names no boards, with the boards still in the archive beside it.
A manifest naming two boards over an archive holding one.
Three boards and a ring that closes over two of them. The third is filed, named by the manifest, and never reached.
A talker document: references and entries with paths, and not one picture behind them.
A picture entry with bytes behind it and no reference beside them.
A key naming a picture its own board does not list.
A recording named by a board and not in the archive.
A key naming a recording its own board does not list.
A recording at 24 kHz. The device does not refuse one - it plays it at 16 - so both halves of this boundary refuse it instead.
A recording under a name layout.bin cannot carry. Refused here, at both ends, rather than at the far end of a build nobody is watching.
A Sammlung with no sets in it. There is no artefact, because there is no package a writer could have written.
